title: Guillain–Barré syndrome mimics primary biliary cirrhosis-related myopathy
case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with end-stage liver disease secondary to primary biliary cirrhosis presented with a 6-week history of rapidly progressive weakness that began after an episode of bronchitis. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and childhood splenectomy. Medications were atorvastatin and metformin. She denied smoking, alcohol use, or illicit drugs.

On examination, she had proximal muscle weakness more pronounced in the lower extremities. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the lower extremities and preserved in the upper extremities. Plantar reflexes were downgoing bilaterally. Cerebellar testing and gait could not be assessed. Rectal tone was intact.

Laboratory studies showed a creatine kinase level of 608 U/L (normal 24–170) and a serum myoglobin of 3850 µg/L (normal <30). Nerve conduction studies demonstrated findings consistent with a myopathy and no evidence of neuropathy or neuromuscular junction disorder. Cerebrospinal fluid protein was within normal limits. 

A muscle biopsy of the anterior thigh revealed numerous fibers with decreased caliber and angulated morphology, occasional fiber necrosis with myophagocytosis highlighted by CD68, scattered CD3-positive T cells, fiber splitting, and occasional regeneration, with no evidence of a primary inflammatory myositis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Guillain–Barré syndrome was considered because of the preceding infection and areflexia — “Our patient presented with a history of infection followed by progressive weakness… physical examination revealed proximal weakness and absent patellar reflexes. These features together are suggestive of GBS.”  
2. PBC-related myopathy was considered given known myositis in PBC — “Myositis is, however, known to occur in PBC patients.”  
3. Elevated muscle enzymes argued against GBS — “Serum CK is only rarely elevated in GBS.”  
4. Anti-mitochondrial antibody–mediated muscle injury supported a primary myopathy — “Circulating anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMAs) in PBC patients are thought to induce muscular injury.”  
5. EMG findings favored a myopathic process over a neuropathy — “nerve conduction studies showed evidence for a myopathy and no evidence for a neuropathy or disorder of the neuromuscular junction.”  
6. Normal CSF protein argued against GBS — “Cerebrospinal fluid protein was not elevated.”  
7. Muscle biopsy necrosis explained elevated enzymes but not weakness, suggesting another cause — “The muscle biopsy showed limited myocyte necrosis, which cannot account for the patient's progressive weakness; however, it could account for the elevated serum CK and myoglobin and EMG findings.”  
8. Angulated fibers on biopsy supported a neurogenic origin of weakness — “Angulated fibers were present and support a neurogenic origin of the patient's weakness.”
